Landing craft, the boats needed to put armies ashore, had become the tightest bottleneck in Allied planning, and Roosevelt wants the numbers at once.

He asks whether the present schedules for building and finishing landing craft can be increased in each month from January through May. Maurice Maeterlinck, the Belgian playwright later famous for The Blue Bird, turned essayist in The Treasure of the Humble in 1896. Against noise, display, and restless ambition, he praises silence, humility, and the unseen inner life. The essays are gentle and dreamlike, reading at times like prose poetry.

Maeterlinck finds spiritual treasure in small, quiet things: a sleeping child, a kept secret, a moment of true silence between people. He argues the soul grows in stillness more than in events. Readers get meditations meant to be read slowly, by a writer who believed the most important part of a life is the part nobody sees.
tob-10793:
Archibald Sayce, an Assyriologist, compared the religions of ancient Egypt and Babylonia in lectures on their gods, temples, and hopes. Two of the world's oldest literate faiths developed side by side, trading ideas across deserts and empires. Sayce brings them into direct contrast.

Creation and flood myths, priesthoods, festivals, and ideas of the afterlife are weighed one civilization against the other. Similarities raise questions about borrowing; differences reveal distinct temperaments. A classic of early comparative religion, the book is now partly superseded by later archaeology, but it remains readable and shows how Victorian scholarship first mapped the ancient Near East's religious world.
tob-9047-57493:
Pliny the Elder, a Roman officer and tireless reader, packed everything he could learn into his Natural History. At thirty-seven books, it is the largest single work to survive from ancient Rome. John Bostock's nineteenth-century translation opens the set with volume one.

Pliny begins with a bold preface and a tour of the cosmos: the shape of the earth, the sun and stars, and the order of the heavens. Geography follows. Nothing learned escapes his net, from tides to eclipses. Later volumes turn to animals, plants, and stones. The whole work shows one mind trying to hold an empire's knowledge.
tob-4093:
Household religion takes rule-book form in the Grihya-Sutras, translated by Hermann Oldenberg for the Sacred Books of the East. Part one of volume twenty-nine covers the rites of the Vedic home. Birth ceremonies, weddings, funerals, and daily offerings each receive exact directions.

The sutras tell the householder which verses to speak, which offerings to pour, and in what order the acts must fall. Scholars prize them because they show religion as families lived it, not as priests theorized it. Ancient India's family life stands here rule by rule. Verified from the 1919 edition, Oldenberg's version serves historians of ritual well.
bloomfield-moore-keely-and-his-discoveri:
Clara Bloomfield-Moore, a wealthy widow from Philadelphia, spent years backing inventor John Worrell Keely and his promised new force. Her 1893 book Keely and His Discoveries pulls together her case for him. It draws on letters and reports on the Keely Motor Company affair.

Keely claimed his machines ran on 'etheric force,' a power drawn from the air itself by tuned vibration. Bloomfield-Moore prints tests, press reports, and pleas from backers who sank money into the scheme. The book is the main record from inside one of the great science frauds of its age. Keely's force was never found by any outside test.
warboys-three-witches-1593:
The Throckmorton children of Warboys shook, cried out, and named the woman they blamed: Alice Samuel. The Most Strange and Admirable Discoverie of the Three Witches of Warboys, printed in 1593, gives the full case. No Elizabethan witch trial is better documented than this one.

The pamphlet prints the girls' fits, the witness statements, and the long road to the gallows for Samuel and her kin. Judges, clergy, and kin all speak in its pages. Readers can trace how child testimony, once believed, left the accused no ground to stand on. Scholars still mine the record for what it shows about proof and fear.
new-england-witches-further-account-1693:
London readers met the Salem crisis in print in 1693, while the New England trials still echoed. A Further Account of the Tryals of the New-England Witches joins the Salem news with Increase Mather's Cases of Conscience. Mather, a leading Boston minister, had turned against the use of spectral proof.

The pamphlet lets English readers weigh the trials as living news, not far-off tale. Mather's part argues that it is better for suspects to go free than for one innocent to die. The pairing shows debate on both sides of the ocean at once. It is the key English print on Salem from its own year.
hale-collection-modern-relations-1693:
Judge Matthew Hale presided over the famed Bury St Edmunds witch trial of 1664, and a 1693 book gathers his thoughts on such cases. A Collection of Modern Relations concerning Witches and Witchcraft is tied to his name. It links Bury with a run of other trials of the age.

The book collects modern cases of witchcraft and adds Hale's own meditation on the Bury trial. A chief judge of England sets out why he held witchcraft to be real and its proof sound. The volume shows the law's highest minds still firm in belief late in the century. It helps explain why trials ran on so long.
roosevelt-wilderness-hunter-1893:
Theodore Roosevelt hunted the Rockies and wrote it up in The Wilderness Hunter of 1893. Tucked in its tales is the Bauman story, told him by an old trapper. Bauman's partner was found dead in camp, his neck broken, with strange tracks all around.

Bauman said a great two-legged beast had stalked them in the woods and killed his friend. Roosevelt tells it straight, as a true tale of the wild, with no wink. The story is now read as the classic first draft of Bigfoot lore. It gains force from the teller: a hard hunter who became a president.
bierce-can-such-things-be-1893:
Ghosts, beasts, and strange deaths fill Ambrose Bierce's tales in Can Such Things Be?, from 1893. One tale hunts a thing no eye can see. One more traces a man's death in a loop of dread and guilt. Each tale ends with a twist.

Bierce writes in crisp, cold prose. He mocks hope and strips each ghost of soft glow. The set builds on his war tales of 1891. It holds a firm place at the root of the weird tale in the United States. Bierce had honed his craft as a news man in the west. He wastes no word, and each twist lands like a trap snapping shut.
judge-ocean-of-theosophy-1893:
William Q. Judge set out the whole creed in plain words in The Ocean of Theosophy, his book of 1893. Judge led the creed's arm in the United States. He saw that new fans drowned in Blavatsky's vast books. He wrote a short, clear guide that a new hand could read in days.

God, soul, karma, and birth past death get a crisp gloss each. The tone is calm and sure, with no show or fluff. Groups still give this book first to new fans. It is the creed's best known school text. Judge wrote with no fee and sought no fame from the book. That plain aim fits the calm, selfless tone on each page here.
hudson-law-psychic-phenomena-1893:
Thomson Jay Hudson split the mind in two in The Law of Psychic Phenomena, his hit book of 1893. Hudson was a law man and news man in the United States. His scheme gives each man two selves: one that thinks and weighs, one that takes bids, holds all past, and can act in trance, dreams, and strange cures at a word.

On that split he builds cures, faith, and tales of ghosts. The book sold in droves and shaped how his land spoke of the hid self. Its terms roamed far past its field. It is a folk text of mind lore.
barry-steve-browns-bunyip-1893:
John Arthur Barry spins bush yarns in Steve Brown's Bunyip, and Other Stories, his set of 1893. Barry wrote of the far south land's coast and bush with a sailor's zest. His title tale turns the bunyip from camp talk to a full tale. The bunyip is the dread swamp beast of settler lore. Men hunt what may not be there in the flesh at all.

Sea tales, gold tales, and bush hunts fill the set. Barry's prose is warm, wry, and full of local hue. The book is a prime store of that land's tale craft. Its bunyip still prowls.
jean-darras-melusine-1393:
Jean d'Arras wrote this romance of Melusine for a French duke in 1393. The text here is the 1895 Early English Text Society print of the Middle English form, set in print by A. K. Donald. Melusine is the famed maid who is part woman, part fish or snake.

She weds a knight on one term: he must not see her on the one day each week. When he breaks the term, she flies off in her strange form and is lost to him. The tale is the root stock of a vast line of fairy bride tales in Europe.
columbus-journal-first-voyage-1493:
Christopher Columbus kept a day book of his first voyage to the New World in 1492 and 1493. What we have is a short form made by Las Casas from the lost first text. Clements Markham turned it into English for the Hakluyt Society in 1893.

Off the Rio del Oro, Columbus notes a sight of 'mermaids' by his crew. His dry line says they were not as fair as tales claim, and he had seen such beasts before. Most now think the beasts were manatees, but the note is the most famed mermaid sight in print.
mather-wonders-invisible-world-1693:
Cotton Mather wrote The Wonders of the Invisible World in 1693. Mather was a Boston priest at the heart of the Salem witch trials. The book gives his own tale of the trials of 1692. It is the most famed first-hand text of the whole dark tale.

Mather tells of the fits of the girls, the tests used, and the trials' course. He prints the tales of five key cases in full. His aim was to back the judges and warn of the Devil's plots. The book is grim proof of how faith and fear drove the trials.
hermetic-museum-vol-2-1893:
A. E. Waite put out The Hermetic Museum, Restored and Enlarged, in 1893. Book Two ends the pair. The Museum is a store of old tracts on alchemy in English dress. Waite was the great voice of the occult age in Britain.

Tracts by famed hands of the art fill the book, some in print for the first time. The texts deal with the stone, the elixir, and the purge of base metals. Waite adds heads and notes to guide the new hand through the maze. The pair is a chief store of the alchemy of the West.
blackstone-commentaries-vol-2-1893:
Sir William Blackstone wrote his Commentaries on the Laws of England in the 1760s. George Sharswood's dress of 1893 fills this book. Book Two of this set holds Books Three and Four of the work. Book Three deals with wrongs to men in their own rights.

Book Four deals with wrongs to the state and the realm at large. Crime, courts, and pains for each fault fill its long run of text. Blackstone's clear prose made English law a thing a plain man could read. The Commentaries shaped law in Britain and the States for a long age.
leopardi-essays-dialogues-1893:
Giacomo Leopardi wrote his Essays and Dialogues in Italian in the 1820s, as the Operette Morali. The ironic dialogues on happiness, nature, and human illusion mark the prose peak of Italian pessimism. Leopardi, a frail scholar-poet of Recanati, finished most of them by the age of twenty-six.

Nature, the Moon, a fashion plate, and a seller of almanacs take turns in brief, lucid scenes. Nature tells an Icelander she neither knows nor cares that men suffer under her vast, blind laws. Pleasure, a dialogue proves, is always past or future, never present to the hand that grasps it. Leopardi's classical polish makes despair elegant, and his humor keeps the gloom from mere negation of life. The dialogues stand beside his great lyrics, the Canti, as his gift to prose.
bradley-appearance-reality-1893:
F. H. Bradley published Appearance and Reality in 1893, the summit of British idealism. Bradley argues that the world as it appears is full of contradictions. Relations, qualities, time, and the self all break down under strict thought. Reality must therefore be one harmonious Absolute that thought can only approach.

The Absolute, for Bradley, is a single experience beyond relations. Finite things are appearances of it, true in degrees. Moore and Russell began their careers by rebelling against this monism. Their revolt shaped analytic philosophy for a century. Bradley's prose is dense but masterful. The book remains the classic statement of British absolute idealism.
mach-mechanics-mccormack-1893:
Ernst Mach was an Austrian physicist who distrusted any idea that could not be tied to what we sense and measure. His Science of Mechanics, first published in German in 1883 and in English in 1893, retells the growth of mechanics as a human story. Thomas McCormack translated this edition.

Mach attacks Newton's talk of absolute space and time as empty words beyond all test. He retells the work of Galileo, Newton, and others as a chain of careful trials and errors. Einstein read Mach closely, and the book helped clear the ground for relativity. He writes history and criticism together, judging each past claim by the tests it passed.
hort-way-truth-life-1893:
Fenton John Anthony Hort was the Cambridge textual critic who, with Westcott, rebuilt the Greek text of the New Testament. His Way, the Truth, the Life, published in 1893, prints his Hulsean Lectures on the words of Jesus in John's Gospel. The book shows the great critic as a theologian.

Hort takes Christ's claim to be the way, the truth, and the life as a key to the whole faith. He reads the Gospel's images of light, bread, and the shepherd as one unfolding self-revelation. The lectures' quiet depth reveals why Cambridge trusted Hort with its hardest textual questions.
orr-christian-view-god-world-1893:
James Orr was a Scottish theologian whose Christian View of God and the World, published in 1893, prints his Kerr Lectures. The lectures offer a comprehensive Christian worldview against the Victorian unbelief of his age. Orr writes for students facing Darwin, biblical criticism, and doubt.

He argues that the Christian view, God as Father ruling a moral world toward redemption, explains more than any rival system. His survey takes in nature, history, sin, and the incarnation as parts of one intelligible whole. The book helped give evangelical thought the very concept of a worldview to defend.
waite-hermetic-museum-vol1-1893:
Arthur Edward Waite, the English occult scholar, edited The Hermetic Museum in 1893 as a restoration of classic alchemical tracts in English. Volume one opens the two-volume set, whose second volume already stands in this library. Waite chose texts he thought held the true thread of Western alchemy.

The tracts speak in the riddling language of the art: green lions, kings in baths, and stones that are not stones. Waite's introductions guide the reader through each author's life and claims with a scholar's patience. The set gave English readers a small library of alchemy between two covers.
partridge-opus-reformatum-1693:
John Partridge was a London astrologer and almanac maker whose Opus Reformatum, published in 1693, offers a reformed astrology. Partridge was a Whig in politics and a scourge of his fellow astrologers in print. His chief target was John Gadbury and the old art Gadbury defended.

He argues that astrology must be rebuilt on Ptolemy's rules alone, swept clean of Arabic additions and English habits. The feud between Partridge and Gadbury filled pamphlets for years and entertained the coffeehouses of London. Swift later mocked Partridge in the famous Bickerstaff hoax, but the Opus shows the reformer in earnest.
revised-odd-fellowship-illustrated-1893:
John Blanchard, a minister and fierce critic of secret societies, published Revised Odd-Fellowship Illustrated in 1893. The Odd Fellows were a large fraternal order with lodges, degrees, and private ritual. Blanchard printed what he said was their full revised ritual so the public could judge it.

Pages give the opening and closing forms, oaths, prayers, songs, and degree work of the lodge, with notes attacking them. Blanchard argued that secret pledges and mock sacred scenes were wrong for Christians. Whether read as warning or record, the book preserves the exact forms of a major fraternal order at the end of the nineteenth century.
tucker-instead-of-a-book-1893:
Benjamin R Tucker published Instead of a Book, by a Man Too Busy to Write One in 1893 in New York. Tucker edited Liberty, the leading journal of individualist anarchism in America. Too busy, as his title jokes, to write a fresh book, he gathered his best pieces from the journal instead.

Essays and sharp exchanges set out his program against what he called the four monopolies: money, land, tariffs, and patents. His key piece, State Socialism and Anarchism, contrasted his free-market anarchism with state socialism. Tucker answered critics at length and in a fighting style. The volume is the fullest record of American individualist anarchism in its editor's own words.
weismann-germ-plasm-1893:
August Weismann was a German biologist who set out to explain how traits pass from one generation to the next. His book appeared in German in 1892 and reached English readers a year later. W. Newton Parker and Harriet Rönnfeldt translated it, and it was published in 1893.

Weismann argued that the body holds two kinds of material. Germ cells carry heredity forward, while the rest of the body, the soma, dies with each person. Because of that split, changes gained during life cannot be inherited by children. His germ-plasm theory shaped early debates about evolution and heredity for years.
gissing-odd-women-1893:
George Gissing published The Odd Women in 1893, taking his title from the many women of his time who could never marry for lack of men. Gissing wrote about the Madden sisters, left poor by their father's sudden death. The novel asks what unmarried women were supposed to do with their lives.

Two sisters scrape by as teachers and shop workers, while their younger sister Monica is courted by an older, controlling man. Nearby, Rhoda Nunn runs a school training women for office work and preaches independence. Love tests every one of these positions. The novel is now read as a founding text about women's work and freedom.
marlowe-massacre-paris-1593:
Christopher Marlowe wrote The Massacre at Paris near the end of his life, dramatizing recent French history. France's wars of religion were still raging when the play reached the stage around 1593. The text that survives is short and may be a cut-down version of what Marlowe wrote.

The Duke of Guise plots the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, when Catholic mobs slaughtered Huguenot Protestants in Paris. Kings rise and fall quickly as assassinations pile up. Marlowe's Guise is a cold, ambitious villain who boasts of his crimes. The play is brutal and hurried, but it shows how raw recent politics could be on the Elizabethan stage.
yeats-celtic-twilight-1893:
William Butler Yeats published The Celtic Twilight in 1893, gathering sketches he had written about the folklore of the Irish west. Yeats was then leading the Irish literary revival, urging writers to draw on their own country's tales. He collected much of this material around Sligo, his mother's home country.

The short pieces record peasants' beliefs in faeries, ghosts, and enchanted places, told in the tellers' own spirit. Yeats neither mocks the beliefs nor simply endorses them. He treats the faery world as a living part of Irish imagination. The book became a source-book for the revival and shaped how Ireland pictured its own past. Its dreamy tone set the mood for a generation of Irish writing.
crane-maggie-1893:
Stephen Crane was twenty-one, poor, and unknown when he published Maggie: A Girl of the Streets at his own expense in 1893. He printed it under a pen name and gave copies away. Crane had prowled New York's Bowery for material and wrote like nothing American fiction had seen.

Maggie Johnson grows up beautiful in a tenement ruled by drink and street fights. A bartender's flash and promises seduce her, then abandon her to the streets her world prepared for her. Crane tells the story in flashing, ironic scenes, with dialogue like stage directions from hell. Nobody in the novel can see Maggie clearly, least of all her family. Maggie is the first unflinching American slum novel and the founding text of literary naturalism here.
jabir-ibn-hayyan-oeuvres-berthelot-1893:
Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Latin as Geber, was the great name of early Arabic alchemy, a scholar of Kufa in the eighth century. A vast body of work bears his name. Marcellin Berthelot printed six of the Arabic treatises in French in 1893, in his study of Arabic alchemy. The text here gives those six.

The treatises set out the sulfur and mercury theory of metals and the search for the elixir that perfects them. Jabir teaches balance, weights, and careful furnace work, a turn toward the measured side of the art. His name ruled alchemy in both Arabic and Latin for centuries. Berthelot's French pages let modern readers meet the Jabirian corpus at its source.
locke-some-thoughts-concerning-education:
John Locke wrote Some Thoughts Concerning Education in 1693, growing out of letters to a friend on raising his son. All 217 sections stand here, in the order Locke gave them. The subject is the making of a gentleman, from a baby's swaddling to a young man's travels.

Health comes first: cold water, plain food, and hard beds build a body fit for life. Virtue follows, then wisdom and breeding, with book learning placed last and lightest. Locke's child learns by practice, example, and love of credit, not by beating and rules. The book shaped English schooling and child rearing for two centuries. Parents still steal from it.
schleiermacher-on-religion-1893:
Friedrich Schleiermacher, a young Berlin preacher, published his Speeches on Religion in 1799 without his name. John Oman's translation of 1893 gives them as On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers. The despisers were his own friends, the educated romantics who thought faith was dead and buried.

Schleiermacher answers that religion is neither dry doctrine nor mere morals. It is intuition and feeling, a sense for the infinite in the finite, tasted before it is argued. That claim refounded modern liberal theology and gave faith a home in feeling. The five speeches still read as a young man's passionate brief for the inner life. Oman made them an English classic.
windelband-history-philosophy-1893:
Wilhelm Windelband wrote his history of philosophy as a history of problems, not just of thinkers. The German book appeared in 1892, and James H. Tufts published his English translation in 1893. Windelband led the Baden school of philosophy in Germany. His aim was a serious textbook on how European thought grew over time.

Windelband shows the motives that pushed each age to form its picture of the world and of human life. Ancient, medieval, and modern thinkers appear as they wrestle with shared questions. Tufts added a short notice on recent English thought for readers of the translation. The result long served students as a compact, clear map of Western philosophy.
stephen-agnostics-apology-1893:
An Agnostic's Apology first appeared as an essay in 1876, and Leslie Stephen later bound it with other essays in 1893. Agnosticism holds that some claims, above all about God, lie beyond what minds can know. Stephen states that position with rare calm and candor. The title essay became a classic Victorian statement of the view.

Around it stand essays on belief, doubt, and the moral life without creed. Stephen refuses both blind faith and cheap scorn for faith. He asks what honesty demands when proof runs out. His prose is dry, clear, and firm. The set still serves readers who want doubt argued well.
besant-autobiography-1893:
Annie Besant told her own story in An Autobiography, printed in 1893. She had been a clergyman's wife, then a famous freethought lecturer beside Charles Bradlaugh. Socialism claimed her next, with strikes and Fabian debates filling those years. In 1889 she met Helena Blavatsky and turned to Theosophy, a turn that stunned her public.

The book ends near that conversion, with her new faith still fresh. Her account is the key primary source for her path to the Adyar society. Later she would lead the Theosophical Society and fight for Indian home rule. The life she records here explains that future. Few Victorian lives changed course so often.
balzac-cesar-birotteau-wormeley-1893:
César Birotteau sells perfume in Paris, dreams of honors, and trusts the wrong men with his money. Balzac's Rise and Fall of César Birotteau, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's 1893 translation, follows a good man's climb and his ruin in bankruptcy court. Commerce, credit, and speculation drive every turn.

Few novels handle a failure of business with such care for law, pride, and shame. Birotteau fights to pay every creditor, though the city shrugs at his fall. The book stands as the Human Comedy's deepest study of trade, the tragedy of an honest shopkeeper in a gaming world.
balzac-physiology-of-marriage-wormeley-1:
Before the great novels, Balzac made his name in 1829 with The Physiology of Marriage, a witty treatise on husbands, wives, and straying hearts. Katharine Prescott Wormeley's 1893 translation keeps its dry, teasing tone throughout. Part satire, part handbook, the book sorts marriages into kinds and warns plainly where each one cracks.

Balzac writes as a doctor of wedlock, counting dangers the way others count pulse beats at a bedside. His jokes rest on sharp watching of Paris drawing rooms and country estates alike. The work founded his Analytic Studies and shows the cool observer who would soon build the Human Comedy.
sienkiewicz-pan-michael-curtin-1893:
The little knight Wołodyjowski makes his last stand at Kamieniec in Pan Michael, the closing volume of Sienkiewicz's Trilogy. Jeremiah Curtin's 1893 translation completes the arc begun in With Fire and Sword and The Deluge. Turkish armies press the Polish border fortress, and the aging hero holds the wall.

Love and loss run beside the siege, as Michael's young wife faces the war he cannot leave. Sienkiewicz wrote to hearten Poles under foreign rule, and his vast battle tales did just that. English readers of Curtin's version meet the national epic of Poland at its heroic close.
cowell-buddha-karita-asvaghosha-1893:
Asvaghosha sang the Buddha's life in Sanskrit verse, and E. B. Cowell's 1893 translation gave English readers the Buddha-Karita whole. The poem, a classical kavya from about the second century, follows the prince from birth and palace luxury to awakening under the tree. Cowell's edition came from the Anecdota Oxoniensia series at Oxford.

Beauty serves doctrine here: every episode turns the hero from the world toward release. The translation was the first complete English rendering of the poem. Readers who want the Buddha's life as India itself told it, in high literary form, start here.
naladiyar-pope-1893:
G. U. Pope translated the Naladiyar for the Clarendon Press in 1893, four hundred Tamil quatrains of Jain teaching. The verses, ascribed to Jain ascetics, school the reader in impermanence: wealth fades, youth passes, and only virtue holds. Pope added critical notes and a concordance, tools he built for students of Tamil.

Each quatrain stands alone, a small, polished warning or comfort. Together they form a breviary of renunciation from early South India, gentler in tone than many such books. Pope's English version remains the classic door into the Naladiyar, a jewel of Tamil didactic verse.
cruden-complete-concordance-1893:
Alexander Cruden, a London bookseller, published the first great English Bible concordance in 1737. The 1893 edition keeps his life and work before the reader. Cruden labored for years, largely alone, indexing the King James text.

Every significant word is listed with the verses where it appears, so readers can gather all the passages on a theme. Cruden adds a summary of the Bible's contents and notes on names and places. His book served preachers and lay readers for two hundred years. It stands beside Strong's as one of the twin pillars of English Bible reference. The 1893 printing adds helps for the growing Sunday school movement.
easton-illustrated-bible-dictionary-1893:
Matthew Easton, a Scottish minister, published his book in 1893. It was the standard one-volume Bible dictionary for ordinary readers. Easton aimed to put sound learning within reach of Sunday school teachers and families.

Entries cover the history, biography, geography, doctrine, and literature of the Bible in plain language. Illustrations, tables of dates, and maps support the articles. Easton takes a conservative line, trusting the text while using the new digging of his day. The dictionary sold widely and was reprinted for decades; digital editions still circulate among students of the scriptures today. The tone is calm and plain, made for home use as much as for the pulpit.
plos-pone-0003393:
Yumi Yamaguchi-Kabata and colleagues mapped a special class of DNA changes in this 2008 paper. A nonsense change puts a stop sign in the middle of a gene's instructions. The protein then ends early and often fails to work. Little was known about where these changes sit in human genes.

The team scanned human gene data for these stop-sign changes, called polymorphisms. They charted how often each one occurs and which genes carry them. They also weighed what the changes do to gene function. The map helps doctors judge which DNA changes are likely to matter.
plos-pone-0003493:

commons-distribution-of-wealth-1893:

The alternative death pathway kills stubborn cancers. A backdoor to tumor-cell death via IMPDH inhibition, repurposing an immunosuppressant against hardy tumors.
plos-pone-0005593: Some people resist norovirus thanks to a genetic mutation. Carlsson and team showed the FUT2 G428A mutation strongly protects against symptomatic norovirus GII-point-4. The secretor-status genes explain outbreak patterns. Genes deciding who gets sick, in a nursing-home outbreak, host genes of infectious disease susceptibility.
plos-pone-0005693: Brain atlases are hard to draw in 3D slices. Modha gave a scheme turning slice-based atlases to a idea outer surface atlas. The opening makes folds clear. Smoothing the brain's wrinkles, as an idea and clearly, brain maps made drawable, a tool for picture outer tangle.
plos-pone-0005793: Water striders wage sexual conflict over mating. Han and Jablonski showed female genitalia concealment boosts intimate male courtship. The coevolutionary arms race favors gentleness. Intimacy winning over coercion, in water striders, sexual conflict's odd outcome, female defenses shaping male conduct.
plos-pone-0006393: Machines can read science papers faster. Barnickel and team used neural nets to pull links from medical texts. The tool speeds lit search — machine reading for readers, trained big, with MEDLINE-scale text tamed. Word-pair methods beaten, knowledge pulling, auto: hours saved.
plos-pone-0006493: A DNA repair enzyme's excess thickens guts. Yoshizawa and team found extra Pol beta drives gut hyperplasia in mice. The repairman's overdrive backfires — too much of a good enzyme, shown, in altered mice. Tumors watched, and human tumors echo it: extra's cost.
plos-pone-0006593: Cancer's hyper gene meets its match. Bhat and team found proteasome blockers strike FoxM1. The busy gene, silenced — tumor's engine, stalled, shown, in clinic or trials. Workings unclear, cranked up in tumors: tumor-driving factor, general target, tumor-fighting action, inhibitors' prize.
plos-pone-0009393: Some colon cancers carry a broken DNA-repair system, a clue that flags Lynch syndrome and guides treatment — but current tests are slow and need extra healthy tissue for comparison. This paper builds a streamlined five-marker DNA test that spots the repair defect from the tumor sample alone. The new assay promises faster, cheaper screening, catching patients who need closer watching or different therapy.
plos-pone-0009493: Brain-controlled prosthetic limbs work better when the computer listens to multiple brain signals at once — but combining them in real time is hard. This paper presents a decision-fusion method that merges different neural data streams as they arrive. The approach pushes brain-computer interfaces toward smoother, more natural control of artificial limbs.
plos-pone-0009593: Jak2 is a key signal relay in immune cells. Mice engineered to lack it in dendritic cells survived a lethal dose of bacterial toxin that triggers septic shock. The paper reveals a single signal protein as a lever on deadly inflammation — and a potential brake for sepsis.
plos-pone-0010393: Bee venom's serine protease does double duty: in insects it triggers immune clotting, in mammals it dissolves blood clots. This study characterizes both roles. The paper reveals a venom enzyme with split personalities across the animal kingdom. Such moonlighting enzymes hint at how venoms evolve new tricks from old tools.
plos-pone-0010493: Stem cells must choose: multiply or specialize. This study shows the REX-1 marker and p38 MAPK activity tip that decision in human mesenchymal stem cells. The paper maps the fork in a stem cell's road. The map helps scientists steer stem cells toward desired fates.
plos-pone-0010593: When yeast cells mate, their membranes must fuse — and the protein Prm1p makes it happen. This study shows Prm1p must pair up into covalent dimers to do its job. The paper reveals the molecular mechanics of cellular union.
plos-pone-0010693: Immune cells vary person to person — and so does disease risk. This study profiles monocyte gene expression to link variation to susceptibility. The paper hunts the genetic roots of immune differences. The data connect gene activity to human illness and treatment response.
plos-pone-0010793: Reading relies on abstract letter codes in the brain. This study combines masked priming with magnetoencephalography to probe how we represent orthography. The paper peers into the reading mind. The findings illuminate the neural basis of literacy. The science could reshape reading instruction.
plos-pone-0010893: Sweden stopped drug-resistant Beijing TB in its tracks. This study finds the feared genotype does not spread locally despite global alarm. The paper delivers reassuring epidemiology. The finding guides targeted public-health action. The containment is a quiet public-health win.
plos-pone-0010993: Tumors bribe immune cells into helping them grow. This study shows the antimicrobial peptide hBD-3 steers tumor-associated macrophages via the CCR2 receptor. The paper models a vicious recruitment loop. Blocking the signal could starve tumors of allies. The loop is a promising drug target.
plos-pone-0011093: Diabetic sugar damage pushes skin cells toward suicide. This study shows a precursor of advanced glycation end products triggers ER-stress-driven caspase-3 activation in human skin cells via NADPH oxidase 4. The paper maps a damage cascade. The finding suggests protective targets.
plos-pone-0011193: The body's fat-release enzyme wears several structural hats. This study examines the quaternary structure and enzymology of different hormone-sensitive lipase isoforms. The paper reveals how form tunes function. The finding informs metabolism science. The structural tuning controls energy release. The release fuels the body between meals.
plos-pone-0011293: Carps and minnows chew with teeth in their throats. This study traces evolutionary trends of pharyngeal dentition in Cypriniformes, one of the most diverse fish orders. The paper reveals how throat teeth evolved. The finding informs fish biology. The informed biology maps biodiversity.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1293:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Ambassador Hornbeck in the Netherlands on 23 July 1945. The message answered the Hague post from Washington, in the circuit of guidance that bound the embassies to the home office during the summit.

Orders to a newly freed country had to match what the talks were deciding in Germany. The home office kept its envoys in step as stands shifted. This cable is that keeping-in-step at work. It preserves a moment in the traffic between the two governments, caught in the American files at the height of the conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1393:
Mikołajczyk wrote another diary entry on 31 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam leaders signed their protocol. His file of papers is the longest single-author run in this section of the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

On the eve of the settlement, a diary entry holds a special charge. The writer knows the decisions are nearly fixed, yet not announced. Mikołajczyk's page for that day lets readers stand where he stood: informed of much, able to change little, still writing. Set against the dry protocol printed nearby, the diary restores the fear and hope that the official text leaves out entirely.
frus-1945-50-intel-d93:
Eddy wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 30 January 1947. The intelligence chief's channel to the department's second-ranking man was by then a well-worn path. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack had used the same channel in the office's first autumn, and Eddy now used it in its steadier second year. Acheson remained the ear that mattered for the department's inner business. Readers can compare the two chiefs' papers to Acheson across fifteen months: the first pleading for an office's life, the second conducting its affairs. That contrast is the State intelligence story in two letters, and the volume prints both ends of it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d193:
A text titled "Circular Instruction From the Department of State" bears the date 15 April 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 193 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

Orders of this kind turned broad policy into daily rules. They name the office in charge and the work to be done. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d293:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Chief of Naval Operations (Denfeld) on 18 June 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 293 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d393:
W. Park Armstrong, the Secretary of State's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter on 2 August 1949. His letter is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series.

Armstrong ran the State Department's own intelligence office, the unit that read world events for the Secretary. A letter from him to the head of the CIA shows the two shops talking at the top. It helps readers see how the State Department tried to keep its own strong voice in intelligence work.
frus-1861-d93:
On 29 October 1861, William H. Seward closed the month with a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 93 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's last October letter to Adams keeps the routine of the autumn intact. Neither man knew that a Union warship was about to stop a British mail ship at sea. The letter's calm close to the month makes the crisis that followed stand out all the more. Within a month the two envoys seized from the Trent would fill every London talk. Every London talk that winter would turn on the names of those two envoys.
frus-1861-d193:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 April 1861. The dispatch is document 193 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton held the St. Petersburg post until Clay could reach it. His April report came four days before Fort Sumter. It shows the old envoy serving the new chief through the last days of peace, with Russia friendly but far away. Russia's goodwill, though real, could not send ships or gold across the world in time. Goodwill that could not send aid still denied aid's hope to the other side.
frus-1861-d293:
The State Department sent word to Mr. Harvey on 30 July 1861, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 293 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d93:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 July 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 93 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d193:
The last Adams letter in this run, Document 193. Is a Seward dispatch of 21 November 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It closes the autumn sequence of the London file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By late November the danger of Britain and France acting together on the war had passed for the year. What remained was the slower fight over ships, trade, and opinion, which ran on into 1863. This letter stands at the point where the record turns from emergency to endurance, a fair summary of the Union's foreign war. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d293:
On 9 July 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 293 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The report came after a gap in the Paris file.

By the time Dayton wrote, news of McClellan's retreat from Richmond was reaching Europe, and French talk of stepping into the war revived. His report from Paris in that week carried the court's first reactions. For Washington, such letters answered a vital question: would failure in Virginia bring foreign action, or only foreign talk? A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d393:
On 16 September 1862, the day before Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg. The dispatch is printed as Document 393 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

A letter to Russia on the eve of the war's bloodiest day could not mention it, and would not be read for weeks. That lag gave the Russian correspondence its reflective tone: policy stated as principle, not reaction. This dispatch closes the Seward-Cameron run in the file, written at the hinge of the autumn campaign. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d493:
On 8 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 493 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Seward wrote two days after Shiloh, though full word of that battle had yet to settle. His orders to The Hague that spring kept returning to the same Dutch questions. Those were port rules and colonial harbors. They also included the standing of Confederate agents in Europe. Pike's task was to be pleasant, exact, and immovable on the Union's rights. The dispatch is one of a steady spring run in the Dutch file, in which neither side let a month pass in silence.
frus-1862-d593:
On 28 June 1862 Thomas Corwin sent this report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 593 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Corwin's end-of-June report came as the Seven Days battles opened in Virginia, though no word of them could reach him for weeks. In Mexico his subject was the French advance and the endurance of the Juárez government, which the Union supported in word. The isolation of his post is part of the record's interest: a minister arguing America's case with month-old news, in a capital itself under threat. His letters home remain the volume's fullest American account of the Mexican crisis of 1862.
frus-1862-d693: On 23 May 1862, a Mr. De Long sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 693 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, his first letter in the file since March of that year. The evidence gives the writer, the date, and the place in the volume, but not his post or what the letter covers.
frus-1863p1-d93:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and a Seward letter shares it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 93 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late February was one of the thickest points in the whole file, with both men writing in bunches. Adams's sheets reported the London scene as the month closed: officials, papers, and Southern men all in motion. This one opens his set of three for the day. The pile itself tells the story of a post at full stretch.
frus-1863p1-d193:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 May 1863. It is document 193 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d293:
The mail from London dated 17 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 293 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

British yards were building two ironclad rams for the Confederacy in the summer of 1863. The fight to stop those ships reached its peak that autumn, filling the London mail. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d393:
A note dated 18 February 1863 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 393 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d493:
Among the day's business on 7 May 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d593:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward on 22 July 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d693:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, on 12 November 1863. The letter stands as document 693 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863, part one of that year's printed papers.

By mid-November the two men had a set rhythm of notes, replies, and fresh notes. That rhythm was itself a kind of peace work. It gave both capitals a calm way to raise sharp points about the war at sea and on land. For the reader, this dispatch fills in one more day of that rhythm. Its plain, brief form is typical of how the work got done.
plos-pbio-0020393:
Mathew T. Pletcher, Philip McClurg, Serge Batalov, and a large team offered a shortcut for mouse genetics in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mapping a trait to a gene in mice normally needs many bred crosses. Their method uses a dense map of DNA markers and computer models to predict the gene's place from strain data alone.

In silico mapping, as they call it, mines the rich records already held on standard mouse strains. It can narrow a trait's location before any new mice are bred. That saves time, money, and animals. The approach works best for traits measured across many strains, and it has become a first pass in mouse gene hunts.
plos-pone-0000093:
Hassan Lemjabbar-Alaoui, Vijay Dasari, Sukhvir S. Sidhu, and their team linked cigarette smoke to lung cancer pathways in PLOS ONE in 2006. Two signal systems, Wnt and Hedgehog, guide lung growth before birth. The team found both systems switched back on by smoke exposure in lung cells, in ways tied to cancer growth.

Dormant growth programs waking up is a common cancer theme. If smoke wakes these two, they become candidate targets for prevention or treatment. The result also helps explain, at the molecular level, why smoking is so potent a cause of lung cancer. It gives tobacco research specific switches to watch in smokers' lung tissue long before tumors form.
plos-pone-0000193:
Michael A. Brockhurst, Nick Colegrave, David J. Hodgson, and colleagues published this experimental evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Working with microcosms, small lab ecosystems of microbes, they test what limits adaptive radiation, the rapid splitting of one lineage into many forms. Their answer is in the title: niche occupation, when the available roles are already filled.

A lineage can only diversify into open ecological space. The authors show experimentally that filled niches block further radiation. The result speaks to grand patterns in evolution, from island finches to bacteria. It does so with a controlled lab test rather than fossil inference alone.
plos-pone-0000293:
Li Chen, Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, and colleagues published this cancer stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Precancerous stem cells sit at the border between healthy tissue and cancer. The authors report that these cells have the potential for both benign and malignant differentiation: they can mature into harmless tissue or into cancer.

A cell that can go either way is both a risk and an opportunity. Understanding what tips it toward cancer could allow prevention at the earliest stage. The paper supports the stem cell model of cancer, in which a small pool of versatile cells drives the disease.
plos-pone-0000393:
Fanny Tzelepis, Pedro M. Persechini, and Mauricio M. Rodrigues examined timing in the immune response in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. CD8 killer T cells destroy infected cells, but they develop with help from CD4 T cells. The team asked how the moment when pathogen numbers rise affects the making of those killer cells.

When an infection grows fast or slowly, the immune system may build its killer force at a different pace or quality. The study varies the timing of the increase in pathogen load and measures the effect on T cell growth and specialization. Results like these matter for vaccine design, where the size and timing of the dose shape the defense that forms.
plos-pone-0000493:
Robert Andrews and Julie Ahringer watched the early sorting machinery of worm embryos, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endosomes are the cell's sorting stations for material taken in from outside. In embryos of the worm C. elegans, the team found an asymmetry of early endosome distribution: the stations are not spread evenly but placed unevenly between the embryo's regions.

Asymmetry is how a one-cell embryo begins building a body with a head end and a tail end. If sorting stations are unevenly placed, the daughter cells may inherit different processing power. The finding adds cell logistics to the list of things embryos set up unevenly from the very first divisions.
plos-pone-0000593:
Sam P. Brown and François Taddei modeled how the lifespan of shared goods changes cooperation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Public goods, from clean water to microbial secretions, invite free-riders who benefit without paying. The authors show that the durability of public goods changes the dynamics and nature of social dilemmas.

A long-lasting good keeps rewarding the group, altering whether cooperation pays and whether cheats prosper. That twist matters from bacteria, where shared enzymes are literal public goods, to human commons like fisheries. Durability is a design lever: goods built to last may sustain the cooperation that produces them.
plos-pone-0000693:
Thomas Efferth, Marco Giaisi, Annette Merling and colleagues tested a malaria drug against resistant leukemia cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drug resistance is a major obstacle in cancer treatment, as tumor cells learn to survive chemotherapy. New drugs are urgently needed that hit tumor cells hard while sparing normal cells. Artesunate, a drug known from malaria care, was their candidate.

The title states their finding: artesunate triggers apoptosis, programmed cell death, in T leukemia cells that resist doxorubicin. The killing runs through ROS, reactive oxygen species that damage cells from inside. Repurposing a known drug for resistant cancers could shorten the road to the clinic.
plos-pone-0000793:
Michel A. Slotman, Aristeidis Parmakelis, Jonathon C. Marshall and colleagues searched mosquito genomes for signs of an arms race, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plasmodium parasites and their mosquito vectors coevolve, which can leave adaptive changes in genes central to the vector's defense. By checking which genes show positive selection in malaria vectors, but not in close non-vector relatives, the team could spotlight the defenses under pressure.

Their title reports evidence for adaptive evolution in LRIM1 in Anopheles arabiensis, one such vector. A gene evolving fast under parasite pressure is a target for intervention. That kind of target hunting is the study's wider promise.
plos-pone-0000893:
Stefan Jonsson, Rebecca LaRue, Mark Stenglein and colleagues tested how a human protein blocks a pig retrovirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, APOBEC3G, is part of the body's built-in defense against viruses. It can stop some retroviruses, including ones that live permanently in animal genomes.

The virus in focus, PERV, lives in pigs and is a concern for transplanting pig organs into people. Using long term cell cultures, the team asked whether APOBEC3G can restrict its spread between species. The work bears on xenotransplantation, using animal organs for human patients. Safety there depends on knowing which human defenses actually hold.
plos-pone-0000993:
Gordon Louie, Thomas Baiga, Marianne Bowman and colleagues solved the structure of basil eugenol synthase, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Phenylpropenes are plant scents that defend leaves and draw pollinators. Eugenol, the scent of cloves and basil, is made by an enzyme that trims a side chain on its starting material.

The team present both the enzyme's structure and its reaction mechanism, how it performs that trim. A structure turns a black box into a machine with visible parts. Plant scent enzymes are also targets for farming and fragrance work. Knowing the mechanism could let growers or chemists tune how much scent a plant makes.
plos-pone-0001093:
Derek Nancarrow, Herlina Handoko, Mitchell Stark and colleagues built a tool to score DNA copy number changes in chip data, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome wide SNP chips can now find where cancer genomes gain or lose DNA stretches, with fine sensitivity. In some tumors those changes are so complex that scoring them by eye fails.

Their tool, SiDCoN, aids that scoring. Copy number changes are not small print: whole gene doses shift, and with them cell behavior. A consistent scorer helps compare tumors across studies. Cancer genome projects produce data faster than humans can grade it, so assistive tools are part of the science, not an extra.
plos-pone-0001193:
Hidden inside many bacterial genomes sit prophages, the dormant genomes of viruses that once invaded the cell. K. V. Srividhya and colleagues present a computer method for finding them in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Prophages help make strains differ, and many genes for bacterial virulence are carried by them.

Their method uses dinucleotide relative abundance difference, a numeric fingerprint of DNA makeup that differs between a bacterium and its prophages. Current methods look for possible viral genes or binding sites and can miss cases. A makeup-based approach offers another way to spot these stowaways. The method needs only the genome sequence itself.
plos-pone-0001293:
Some genes are expressed from only one of the two copies a person carries, the other copy staying silent. Jinhui Wang and colleagues searched the mouse central nervous system for such monoallelic expression, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genes like these are hard to detect, yet the inheritance patterns of several major disorders hint that they are involved.

DNA methylation in regulatory regions is often a mark of the silent copy, which the authors used as a guide. Finding multiple genes with monoallelic expression in the CNS widens the known reach of this phenomenon in the brain. It may matter for disorders with puzzling inheritance.
plos-pone-0001393:
Renat Shaykhiev, Jürgen Behr, and Robert Bals published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how airway cells heal. The cells that line the airways meet germs each day and sense them with alarm proteins. Those alarms are often tied to swelling and harm. The team asked whether the same alarms also help repair.

They found that germ patterns sensed by two such alarms aid growth and repair of the airway lining. The signals helped cells close wounds and stay alive. That dual role shifts the view of these alarms as pure threats. It suggests future drugs might boost the repair side while still curbing harm from infection.
plos-pone-0001493:
Fiona Thompson and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on a malaria shot that mixes two plans. Past work held that the best shot would hit the parasite at more than one life stage. This phase 2a trial was the first to merge two such plans in one shot. Volunteers were then exposed to malaria in a controlled test.

The team report signs that the shot worked at the blood stage of the parasite. Blood stage action is what stops illness once infection starts. Even partial proof at this stage is a gain for the field. It backs the multi stage tack for the next round of shot design.
plos-pone-0001593:
Zoltán Bochdanovits and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on guessing gene pairs that work as a team. Our genome holds few genes for the vast range of traits we show. Gene teams that interact could explain that range. The team sought such teams in patterns of gene change between mice and men.

Pairs whose change patterns track each other are flagged as likely partners. The method scans the whole genome at once, not pair by pair in the lab. Its calls give bench labs a short list to test. True pairs found this way would enrich the map of how traits are built.
plos-pone-0001693:
Momiao Xiong, Frank C. Arnett, Xinjian Guo, and their co-authors studied skin cells from scleroderma patients in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Scleroderma hardens skin and connective tissue. Diseases in general arise when whole biological systems, not single parts, are pushed off balance by environmental triggers, and those systems keep changing over time.

The team disturbed fibroblasts, the cells that build connective tissue, with changes in their environment and tracked how patient and healthy cells responded. They found the dynamic responses differ, per the paper's title. The full text gives the perturbation tests and the response patterns. Distinct response dynamics could become a way to spot the disease's state or test drugs, beyond static gene lists.
plos-pone-0001793:
Kristoffer Ström, Ola Hansson, Stéphanie Lucas, and their co-authors studied fat cells in mice lacking a fat-splitting enzyme, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Hormone-sensitive lipase, or HSL, works mainly in adipose tissue. There it breaks down stored triglycerides and diglycerides to mobilize fatty acids when hormones call for energy. It also acts on a broad range of other substrates.

In mice with no HSL, white adipocytes, the usual storage cells, attained features of brown adipocytes, the heat-producing kind. The full text gives the fat tissue measurements and gene markers. White fat turning brown-like is a sought-after effect in obesity research, since brown fat burns energy as heat.
plos-pone-0001893:
Haoran Wang and co-authors studied the high squeaks mice make during courtship, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Adult mice call at pitches too high for human ears when they seek mates, yet the genes that steer such calls were little known. The team worked with mice that lack one of several signal proteins in the brain.

They tested mice missing muscarinic receptors M2, M4, or M5, and mice missing the D2 dopamine receptor. Sex cues and a dose of amphetamine were used to prompt calls. By counting calls in each line, the study ties brain signal paths to a basic social act. That helps map how genes and brain chemistry shape voice and courtship.

Thomas Taylor translated Sallustius's On the Gods and the World into English in 1793. Sallustius, a fourth-century Roman official, wrote a short catechism of pagan belief. Taylor bundled it with the Pythagoric Sentences of Demophilus and hymns of Proclus.
